The erratic course of our weather since last fall brings to mind the fact that we spend
most of our lives anticipating certain experiences or trying to achieve certain goals.
Whatever may be the ultimate outcome of these hopes and accomplishments we man
age to accept the good with the bad. The disappointments are often offset by the high
points that follow these dour moments. There seems to be some kind of balance in the
lives of men which makes all of this possible.
Did it ever occur to you that keeping in touch with those who spent their young
years with you as undergraduate members of your chapter of Psi Upsilon might mean
an extension of those pleasant years far beyond those original four years? Why should
any of us get so involved in our daily Uving that we lose track of those Brothers with
whom we lived and worked away back then? To Owlie it doesn't make very much sense.
His experience has been just the opposite. Those attachments have remained real and
personal. They have made Ufe something extra for him.
OwUe is well aware that the various paths which we follow after we have left those
"Halls of Ivy" are many and varied. It may be difficult, at times, to be close to any of
your fellow Brothers. But there are many substitutes for keeping close to Psi U. You
could make up your mind to be a regular member of your Chapter's Alumni Association.
The cost is seldom more than a couple of drinks at the local bar. This is offered as one
step in the right direction.
In many parts of the country there exist Psi Upsflon Associations. These are made up
of those Psi U's who live in the area and discover that they can become a part of the
alumni circle of Psi Upsflon. They meet their equals from many Chapters and get to
know how very different each Chapter may h^ve seemed to be and yet how very much
the same they aU are. When gathered together, they represent a cross section of that
which you found so valuable and wanted in your own Chapter.
Some day soon OwUe hopes that there wUl be issued a catalogue of all of the living
members of our
Fraternity. The reason for this is that in almost every city and hamlet
�of our country there are Psi U's who live next door, or down the block from one an

Food for Thought
Some years back there was a Roman Senator who
gained considerable fame as an orator. Some of us
may remember him as part of the Latin courses we
had to endure in our pre-coUege days.
At any rate Cicero, for that was his name, was wont
to turn a few phrases during his orations which sur
vive today. One of these was:
"Our greatest glory is not in never failing but in
rising every time we fall."
Doubtless some of us, some of our Chapters and
some of our Alumni Associations have had those
"down-points." Nearly always there is an underlying
reason for this "failing." It should be of comfort to
know that the wisdom of Cicero says to us, "Rise
again; that is the first step to success and glory."

In 1835, at the fledgling University of the City of
New York (known now by its name of New York
University), a group of students attending classes in
the new building became interested in the new stu
dent interest�the Greek Letter Society. They had
learned that there were four such at Union College
in Schenectady, New York. The four included Kappa
Alpha Society, Sigma Phi, Delta Phi, and Psi Upsilon.
The last was only two years old but it had established
itself as a society which was primarily interested in
the development of its members and less interested in
such things as finding the most prestigious students for
membership.
This interest came about primarily because one
Jeremiah Skidmore Lord had entered Union College
in January, 1834 and was initiated as a member of
Psi Upsilon the following month. The following year
he transferred to New York University. Another stu
dent, Isaac Dayton, started at N.Y.U. but transferred
to Union in 1835 and was initiated into Psi Upsilon
there that fall. It was Brother Dayton who conceived
of the idea of a branch at the New York institution and
entered into communication with Brother Lord.

As early as 1836 the local society of Psi Upsilon of
Union College had selected a committee to review the
possibility of expansion. Sigma Phi had already estab
lished a branch at Hamilton College nearby. It was
reported that Alpha Delta Phi, founded at Hamilton,
was looking around for a place to begin an expansion
program. The Psi Upsilon committee came to the con
clusion that the University of the City of New York
was the ideal place to start.
Negotiations were carried forward but were slow due
to the lack of any form of rapid communication be
tween the two groups. It is a matter of record that "the
Embryo Branch of the Psi Upsilon Society" was or
ganized on December 6, 1836. Formal approval by the
Society at Union came the next month, and the Chap
ter to be known as the Delta officially was inducted in
to the society on February 11, 1837.
Once the Delta Chapter was established the mem
bers became inspired with an aUnost missionary zeal
to spread the good word. It is known that the estab
lishment of the Lambda Chapter at Columbia Uni
versity was the direct result of the efforts of the Delta
Brothers. This same spirit was carried throughout
New England and it has been noted that the bearers
of this active interest in the Greek Letter Society had
much to do with the estabUshment of the chapters at
Yale, Brown, Amhurst, Dartmouth, Bowdoin, Harvard,
and, somewhat later. Trinity.
One interesting fact in the history of the Delta
Chapter is that it had selected its first home prior to
the ultimate approval by the Chapter at Union Col-

lege. The latter had selected Theta as its name when it
approved Delta for the first branch operation. The
building was located opposite the southeastern side

The property on which it stood would now be the

New York University.
Although Alpha Delta Phi had come to Washing
ton Square two years before the Delta, it did not flour
ish for long. For two years, 1839 to 1841, Psi Upsilon
was the only Greek Letter Society on the campus. Del
ta Phi then expanded to N.Y.U., and Zeta Psi was
founded there in 1847.
When the CoUege of Arts and Science moved to
University Heights in 1892 Psi Upsilon went with the
move. A drive was held to raise funds to build a new
Chapter House. At the time Frank J. Gould, the son
of the railroad magnate, was a member of the Chap
ter. Through his aegis and financial support the first
wholly owned fratemity house appeared on the up
town campus. It was the home of the Delta Chapter.
While this building was being erected the Chapter
made its home directly across the street from the new
home, where the members could watch the replica of
an old Revolutionary Inn unfold as one of the first,
if not the first, such building erected and designed
ideally for fraternity Uving.
After flourishing for over seventy-five years at the
"Heights" the Delta was faced with its most serious
challenge. It had been able to weather World Wars I
and II as well as the Korean War. Now the arts col
lege was to be retumed to Washington Square because
the University was compelled to sell the Bronx prop
erty in order to continue in existence. The sad result
of this decision to sell marked the closing of all but

Brother HoUday is president of the Armco Steel Cor

By 1968 he had been elected vice president for the

As an undergraduate at the University of Michigan
